Vietnamese.notes: SOUNDS: Vietnamese is a tonal language (6 tones are used in Viet Nam); English has no tones. There are three major dialects (Northern, Central, Southern) with different consonants, vowels, and tones, so ask the family which dialect the child speaks. English consonants not found in standard Vietnamese include /ɡ θ ð ʃ ʒ tʃ dʒ ɹ/ (sources differ slightly on /ɡ ʃ ʒ/, likely due to dialect), so errors on these in English may reflect first-language influence rather than a speech disorder. DEVELOPMENT: Northern Vietnamese-speaking children had acquired nearly all Vietnamese sounds and tones by about age 5;5 to 5;11. Exceptions were initial /ɲ, s, z, x/, the semivowel /w/ within syllables, and tones 3 (ngã) and 4 (hỏi), so errors on these may still be typical before age 6. This study covered the Northern dialect only. LANGUAGE: In a 4-year study of school-age Vietnamese-English children in the US, both languages grew, but English grew faster, so many children shifted toward English dominance, and receptive and expressive skills followed different patterns. Lower Vietnamese skills compared to English may reflect this shift, not a disorder. Parents' use of Vietnamese supported children's Vietnamese vocabulary and did not slow their English vocabulary. TOOLS: Vietnamese Speech Assessment (Phạm, Le, & McLeod, 2016); Multilingual Assessment Instrument for Narratives (MAIN), Vietnamese version; Intelligibility in Context Scale (ICS), Vietnamese version.
